title: A Letters for the Postcard
premise: For ten years, Noor Villalobos has exchanged unsigned letters with a stranger through a postcard service meant for the grieving — a correspondence that became the only steady thing in her life. When her café faces foreclosure and a new neighbor, Elian Reyes, moves in next door, Noor slowly realizes he is her letter-writer: he wrote to survive his sister's death, and she answered without knowing it. As the bank's deadline closes in and their unspoken truth strains between them, both must risk saying the sentence they've rehearsed for a decade. In the end, the community Noor unknowingly built rallies to save the café, and she and Elian finally sign their names — choosing each other not as an escape from loss, but as proof they survived it.
about_author: Kestrel Dunmore is the pen name of a former bakery counter worker who spent six years writing letters to strangers through grief-support postcard services before turning the experience into fiction. They live in a coastal town where they still bake on Sundays and answer every letter by hand.

chapters.title: The Last Invoice
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Opening on the morning the third final notice arrives, Noor runs her café on muscle memory while hiding the letters from the bank taped inside her register. Emotional beat: weary denial — she measures her life in payments due, not years lived.

chapters.title: Postmark 2015
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, flashback woven into present. We learn how a grief-postcard service paired her, after her mother's death, with an anonymous writer whose words kept her standing. Emotional beat: tenderness for a stranger who never signed a name.

chapters.title: The Man with the Moving Boxes
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Elian Reyes moves into the apartment above the shuttered florist next door; he orders coffee every morning, lingers too long, and flinches when Noor mentions handwriting. Emotional beat: uneasy curiosity sharpening into recognition she refuses to voice.

chapters.title: What He Carried
chapters.summary: Elian's POV. We learn his side: ten years of letters written after his sister Marisol drowned, never knowing the recipient was the woman downstairs. Emotional beat: guilt — he chose her neighborhood deliberately and hasn't confessed why.

chapters.title: Flour and Confession
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. A power outage traps them in the dark café over proofing dough; near-confessions surface but break off. Meanwhile the bank offers a buyout to the developer eyeing the block. Emotional beat: intimacy that feels like betrayal of the secret.

chapters.title: The Sentence Rehearsed
chapters.summary: Elian's POV. Elian drafts the letter he's rewritten a hundred times — 'It was me, all along' — and burns it instead. Noor finds a scrap in the shared trash and recognizes the phrasing from letter forty-one. Emotional beat: dread blooming into certainty.

chapters.title: Foreclosure Friday
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The bank representative arrives; the developer's offer stands; regulars begin quietly organizing behind Noor's back. She confronts Elian mid-crisis and accuses him of stalking her grief. Emotional beat: fury as armor against heartbreak.

chapters.title: Letter One Hundred and Twelve
chapters.summary: Elian's POV. Devastated, Elian finally sends the unsent letter through the old postcard service — the last one it will ever forward. Noor reads it at the closing table as the developer waits. Emotional beat: the rehearsed sentence spoken at last, ten years late.

chapters.title: The Block That Stayed
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The community Noor fed for a decade — the florist, the schoolkids, the night-shift nurses — crowds the bank lobby with a crowdfunded counter-offer and a petition. Emotional beat: belonging made visible; found family refusing to let go.

chapters.title: Signed, At Last
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, epilogue in spring. The café reopens under a new sign bearing both their names; two chairs sit by the window where the letters began. They write one final postcard to Marisol's memory and mail it together. Emotional beat: survival reframed — not the price paid, but the people kept.
